title: What this lab is
text: The Virtual Neuro Lab runs experiments on simulated fruit fly (Drosophila) nervous systems wired from real connectome scans. Pages: Neuron Silencing Screen (switch off one neuron; Discovery Screen predictions with confidence levels), Parkinson's (where the dopamine signal is lost as dopamine neurons die), Vivarium (Fly: a body from a micro-CT scan, NeuroMechFly, run by the FlyWire brain; mix tastes or touch her antennae to see feeding and antennal grooming and which brain regions respond; plus Round 1, the calibration test and the lab notebook), Fly Atlas (brain regions and cell types; the Prediction check is linked from it), The worm (C. elegans, 302 neurons), What's next (the plan: docking is the next step). The lab is a hypothesis generator on the road to drug discovery. Experiments run on the FlyWire brain (female, 139,255 neurons, v783) using the published leaky integrate-and-fire model of Shiu et al. 2024 (Nature 634:210) with its published settings; rules for passing are saved before every run.

title: MN9 (tongue motor neuron)
text: MN9 is the motor neuron that extends the fly's proboscis (its tongue) to feed or drink. The lab reads MN9 firing as "tongue out" when it fires 10 or more times per second. There are two MN9s, one per side. Gordon & Scott 2009 (Neuron 61:373) showed it drives proboscis extension.

title: Usnea, Phantom, Fudog, Bract, Roundup, G2N-1 (named feeding neurons)
text: Named neurons in the fly's gnathal ganglion (the feeding centre under the brain) studied by Shiu et al. 2024 and earlier work. Usnea responds to water; Fudog responds to water; Bract and Roundup are needed for drinking; G2N-1 is not; Usnea and Phantom can drive proboscis extension when switched on.

title: Calibration test
text: Before any experiment, the simulated brain must reproduce a known result: sugar taste makes MN9 fire, more sugar more firing, bitter alone does not, bitter cancels sugar, water works, and activity stays contained. The FlyWire brain passed all six rules, so every experiment runs on it. Experiments on Maxime and Hagrid are in progress.

title: Pre-registration (rules saved before the run)
text: For every test the lab saves the question, the real-fly result, and the pass/fail rule with a timestamp before running. Nothing is changed after the run, and misses stay on the page. A fingerprint code on each card changes if the engine, wiring or rules are edited.

title: The simulation model (leaky integrate-and-fire)
text: Each neuron adds up pushes from the neurons wired to it; when its voltage crosses a threshold it fires and resets. Every synapse gives the same small push (0.275 mV), positive or negative depending on the sending neuron's chemical (GABA and glutamate inhibit). Published by Shiu et al. 2024 (Nature 634:210); in that study 91% of 164 predictions tested in living flies held up. Limits: no graded (non-spiking) neurons, no neuromodulators, no body.

title: Connectome, FlyWire, BANC, male CNS
text: A connectome is a map of every neuron and synapse, traced from electron-microscope scans. FlyWire (female brain, 139,255 neurons) is the brain the experiments run on. BANC (Maxime, female brain and nerve cord) and the male CNS (Hagrid, male brain and nerve cord) are the lab's two flies.

title: Vivarium: Fly and her behaviours
text: The Vivarium shows Fly, the lab's fly: a 3D body from NeuroMechFly (Lobato-Rios et al. 2022, Nature Methods), reconstructed from a micro-CT scan of a real fruit fly, run by the FlyWire brain. Choose a stimulus and see which brain regions respond and what she does. Only two behaviours are shown, because only their control neurons are read out and checked against real flies: feeding (tongue out when MN9 fires 10+ times per second) and antennal grooming (when aBN1 fires 5+ times per second; aBN1 starts antennal grooming in real flies, Hampel et al. 2015). Walking, escape, flight and courtship song are not modelled yet: walking and flight are coordinated in the nerve cord, which FlyWire does not include; escape needs visual input not yet tested; only males sing and FlyWire is female. The movements are animations of the behaviour the brain's output calls for; the body is not simulated. title: Region optic (Optic lobe)
text: optic Optic lobe: vision. The two big visual centres behind the eyes. Signals from the photoreceptors pass layer by layer through the lamina, medulla, lobula and lobula plate, which pull out contrast, colour, motion and object features before sending them on to the central brain. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 4463630}, Hagrid {'synapses': 31411837}.

title: Region LA (Lamina)
text: LA Lamina: first visual layer. The first layer behind the eye. Each of about 800 'cartridges' collects input from the R1–6 photoreceptors that look at one point in space and passes it to lamina neurons L1–L5. Counts: Maxime None, Hagrid {'synapses': 318834, 'neurons': 10762, 'left': 117415, 'right': 201419}.

title: Region ME (Medulla)
text: ME Medulla: early vision: contrast, colour, motion. The largest visual region, built of about 800 columns and ten layers. Colour photoreceptors R7 and R8 end here, and its circuits start computing contrast, colour and the direction of motion. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 2928364, 'neurons': 67228, 'left': 1184834, 'right': 1743530}, Hagrid {'synapses': 18681783, 'neurons': 85152, 'left': 8358660, 'right': 10323123}.

title: Region AME (Accessory medulla)
text: AME Accessory medulla: small optic region; clock-neuron hub. A small region at the front edge of the medulla. Clock neurons that make the neuropeptide PDF branch here and receive light information that helps reset the daily clock. The clock itself is a network of about 240 neurons spread across the brain (the count from the FlyWire connectome; older textbooks say about 150). Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 4139, 'neurons': 376, 'left': 1852, 'right': 2287}, Hagrid {'synapses': 27481, 'neurons': 505, 'left': 5703, 'right': 21778}.

title: Region LO (Lobula)
text: LO Lobula: visual features and objects. A deeper visual region that detects features such as small moving objects and looming. Its lobula columnar (LC) neurons carry these features to glomeruli in the central brain. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 831538, 'neurons': 37016, 'left': 360616, 'right': 470922}, Hagrid {'synapses': 8041134, 'neurons': 51998, 'left': 3481644, 'right': 4559490}.

title: Region LOP (Lobula plate)
text: LOP Lobula plate: direction of motion. Receives direction-selective motion signals from T4 and T5 cells, one layer per direction. Large tangential cells here sense whole-field motion (optic flow) used to keep the fly on course. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 699589, 'neurons': 21326, 'left': 296254, 'right': 403335}, Hagrid {'synapses': 4342605, 'neurons': 27083, 'left': 1850091, 'right': 2492514}.

title: Region AL (Antennal lobe)
text: AL Antennal lobe: smell, first stop. The first smell centre, with about 50 glomeruli. Each glomerulus collects the smell neurons that carry one type of odour receptor; projection neurons then carry the signal to the mushroom body and lateral horn. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 990557, 'neurons': 5683, 'left': 503736, 'right': 486821}, Hagrid {'synapses': 2918760, 'neurons': 4767, 'left': 1340846, 'right': 1577914}.

title: Region LH (Lateral horn)
text: LH Lateral horn: inborn smell responses. Receives smell information from the antennal lobe and drives built-in (unlearned) reactions, such as attraction to food odours or avoidance of danger smells. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 151180, 'neurons': 5085, 'left': 63964, 'right': 87216}, Hagrid {'synapses': 1032499, 'neurons': 6457, 'left': 451992, 'right': 580507}.

title: Region MB (Mushroom body)
text: MB Mushroom body: learning and memory. The fly's learning centre. Kenyon cells receive smell (and some visual and taste) information in the calyx and send long axons through the pedunculus into the lobes. There, dopamine neurons signal reward or punishment and output neurons read out the learned value. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 220993}, Hagrid {'synapses': 1713757}.

title: Region MB_CA (Mushroom body calyx)
text: MB_CA Mushroom body calyx: learning centre input. Where projection neurons carrying smell (and some visual and taste) information connect to the Kenyon cells of the mushroom body. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 180575, 'neurons': 5347, 'left': 86376, 'right': 94199}, Hagrid {'synapses': 456939, 'neurons': 4700, 'left': 209202, 'right': 247737}.

title: Region MB_PED (Mushroom body pedunculus)
text: MB_PED Mushroom body pedunculus: Kenyon cell axon bundle. The stalk of Kenyon cell axons running from the calyx to the lobes. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 11509, 'neurons': 2957, 'left': 4523, 'right': 6986, 'note': "Maxime's export assigns very few synapses to the mushroom-body lobes compared with the calyx; this is probably how the BANC export labels these regions, not biology."}, Hagrid {'synapses': 104512, 'neurons': 5218, 'left': 48277, 'right': 56235}.

title: Region MB_VL (Mushroom body vertical lobe)
text: MB_VL Mushroom body vertical lobe: learning output. One of the output lobes. Dopamine neurons here signal reward or punishment, changing how Kenyon cells talk to mushroom-body output neurons. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 20892, 'neurons': 3076, 'left': 11810, 'right': 9082, 'note': "Maxime's export assigns very few synapses to the mushroom-body lobes compared with the calyx; this is probably how the BANC export labels these regions, not biology."}, Hagrid {'synapses': 297677, 'neurons': 4693, 'left': 142687, 'right': 154990}.

title: Region MB_ML (Mushroom body medial lobe)
text: MB_ML Mushroom body medial lobe: learning output. The other output lobe, organised like the vertical lobe into compartments, each with its own dopamine and output neurons. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 8017, 'neurons': 2018, 'left': 2979, 'right': 5038, 'note': "Maxime's export assigns very few synapses to the mushroom-body lobes compared with the calyx; this is probably how the BANC export labels these regions, not biology."}, Hagrid {'synapses': 854629, 'neurons': 6129, 'left': 460479, 'right': 394150}.

title: Region CX (Central complex)
text: CX Central complex: navigation and heading. A chain of midline structures that keep track of which way the fly is facing and help it steer toward goals. It holds the fly's internal compass. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 415870}, Hagrid {'synapses': 2180852}.

title: Region EB (Ellipsoid body)
text: EB Ellipsoid body: heading compass. A ring-shaped structure where E-PG neurons keep a 'bump' of activity that tracks the fly's heading, like an internal compass. Ring neurons bring in visual landmarks. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 112554, 'neurons': 690, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}, Hagrid {'synapses': 652120, 'neurons': 590, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}.

title: Region PB (Protocerebral bridge)
text: PB Protocerebral bridge: heading map relay. A bar-shaped structure where the heading signal from the ellipsoid body is laid out left-to-right and passed to other central-complex neurons. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 62377, 'neurons': 634, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}, Hagrid {'synapses': 158924, 'neurons': 770, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}.

title: Region FB (Fan-shaped body)
text: FB Fan-shaped body: goal-directed steering; sleep. The largest central-complex structure. It combines heading with travel direction and goals to guide steering, and some of its layers help control sleep. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 208450, 'neurons': 2895, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}, Hagrid {'synapses': 1201153, 'neurons': 2677, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}.

title: Region NO (Noduli)
text: NO Noduli: self-motion input. Small paired structures under the fan-shaped body that bring self-motion (speed and turning) signals into the central complex. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 32489, 'neurons': 529, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}, Hagrid {'synapses': 163428, 'neurons': 589, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}.

title: Region AB (Asymmetrical body)
text: AB Asymmetrical body: small, one-sided structure. A small structure near the fan-shaped body, usually larger on one side. It has been linked to long-term memory, but its role is not well understood. Counts: Maxime {'merged_into': 'FB'}, Hagrid {'synapses': 5227, 'neurons': 205, 'left': 943, 'right': 4284}.

title: Region LX (Lateral complex)
text: LX Lateral complex: steering; compass input. Paired regions next to the central complex. The bulb feeds visual cues into the compass, the gall links to compass neurons, and the lateral accessory lobe sends steering signals to descending neurons. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 378708}, Hagrid {'synapses': 1411129}.

title: Region LAL (Lateral accessory lobe)
text: LAL Lateral accessory lobe: steering commands. Receives central-complex output and connects to descending neurons that turn the fly while walking or flying. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 360381, 'neurons': 3949, 'left': 176652, 'right': 183729}, Hagrid {'synapses': 1375008, 'neurons': 5516, 'left': 727487, 'right': 647521}.

title: Region BU (Bulb)
text: BU Bulb: visual cues into the compass. Relays visual information such as landmarks, the sun and polarised light from the anterior optic tubercle to the ring neurons of the ellipsoid body. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 5343, 'neurons': 449, 'left': 2448, 'right': 2895}, Hagrid {'synapses': 36121, 'neurons': 589, 'left': 18003, 'right': 18118}.

title: Region GA (Gall)
text: GA Gall: compass-circuit partner. A small region where certain ellipsoid-body/protocerebral-bridge columnar neurons connect; part of the navigation loop. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 12984, 'neurons': 509, 'left': 5729, 'right': 7255}, Hagrid {'merged_into': 'LAL'}.

title: Region SNP (Superior neuropils)
text: SNP Superior neuropils: senses meet internal state. The top of the central brain, where smell, taste and other senses are combined with hunger, thirst and learned value. Many mushroom-body output and dopamine neurons connect here. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 407816}, Hagrid {'synapses': 4487271}.

title: Region SLP (Superior lateral protocerebrum)
text: SLP Superior lateral protocerebrum: smell and metabolic state. Next to the lateral horn. Receives smell information and links it with signals about the body's nutritional state. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 78770, 'neurons': 5410, 'left': 37358, 'right': 41412}, Hagrid {'synapses': 1763004, 'neurons': 11985, 'left': 815835, 'right': 947169}.

title: Region SIP (Superior intermediate protocerebrum)
text: SIP Superior intermediate protocerebrum: learned value. A zone where mushroom-body output neurons and dopamine neurons connect, linking learned value to behaviour. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 55428, 'neurons': 3958, 'left': 22161, 'right': 33267}, Hagrid {'synapses': 863759, 'neurons': 7619, 'left': 432009, 'right': 431750}.

title: Region SMP (Superior medial protocerebrum)
text: SMP Superior medial protocerebrum: internal state and feeding. A large midline region that integrates hunger, thirst and other internal states with learned and sensory information; many neurosecretory and mushroom-body-related neurons connect here. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 273618, 'neurons': 6046, 'left': 132039, 'right': 141579}, Hagrid {'synapses': 1860508, 'neurons': 9125, 'left': 950400, 'right': 910108}.

title: Region INP (Inferior neuropils)
text: INP Inferior neuropils: integration; largely uncharted. Regions around the mushroom-body lobes and the midline. They are heavily wired but their jobs are still poorly understood. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 693816}, Hagrid {'synapses': 2880543}.

title: Region CRE (Crepine)
text: CRE Crepine: around the mushroom-body lobes. Wraps the mushroom-body lobes and holds many mushroom-body output and dopamine neuron branches. title: Region VLNP (Ventrolateral neuropils)
text: VLNP Ventrolateral neuropils: visual and hearing features. The sides of the central brain, where visual projection neurons from the optic lobe and hearing/wind neurons from the antenna arrive and are processed into features like looming objects or courtship song. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 1722475}, Hagrid {'synapses': 11825397}.

title: Region AOTU (Anterior optic tubercle)
text: AOTU Anterior optic tubercle: visual features to the compass. Receives visual features such as colour and polarised light from the optic lobe and passes them on, via the bulb, toward the central-complex compass. title: Region AVLP (Anterior ventrolateral protocerebrum)
text: AVLP Anterior ventrolateral protocerebrum: hearing and vision. A large region processing auditory information (including courtship song) and visual features. title: Region PVLP (Posterior ventrolateral protocerebrum)
text: PVLP Posterior ventrolateral protocerebrum: visual objects and looming. Where many lobula columnar neurons end in glomeruli, each signalling a visual feature such as a looming object. text: PLP Posterior lateral protocerebrum: visual features. Another major target of visual projection neurons from the optic lobe. title: Region VMNP (Ventromedial neuropils)
text: VMNP Ventromedial neuropils: routes to descending neurons. The lower middle of the central brain. Receives taste input from the mouthparts and legs, contains motor neurons for feeding, and is a major source and target of descending neurons. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 1077570, 'neurons': 9774, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}, Hagrid {'synapses': 3923843, 'neurons': 10357, 'left': 0, 'right': 0}.

title: Region VNC (Ventral nerve cord)
text: VNC Ventral nerve cord: legs, wings, neck, abdomen. The fly's equivalent of a spinal cord, in the thorax. It holds the motor circuits for walking and flight and receives touch and position sense from the body. In the BANC and male CNS scans it is wired to the brain. Counts: Maxime {'synapses': 6370796}, Hagrid {'synapses': 18621085}.

title: What we infer and why it matters (Vivarium)
text: id="infer">What we infer, and why it matters What these results tell us Much of taste behaviour is written in the wiring. With nothing but the scanned connections and one simple rule for how neurons fire, the brain gets the basics right: sugar brings the tongue out, more sugar pushes harder, bitter alone does nothing, and water works through its own neurons. Bitter is built to win. Here, bitter cuts the sugar response from 65 to 0.1 firings a second, and with strong bitter, even double-strength sugar barely gets through (11 a second). A "safety first" design, which makes sense: tasting poison should overrule wanting food. Signals add up. Sugar and water together push the tongue neuron harder than either alone (83 vs 65 for sugar). Wiring isn't the whole story. The brain passed 10 of 15 checks. Results driven by whole groups of sensory neurons came out right; the misses all involve single named neurons. Something beyond the wiring, such as chemical signals for hunger or thirst, seems to shape those. How this can help in the real world Fewer animal experiments. A brain that passes known checks can be used to try ideas first, so real labs only test the most promising ones. The Neuron Silencing Screen does exactly this. Trust, measured. Brain simulations are becoming a common research tool. Scoring one honestly against known results, misses included, shows when its predictions are worth acting on. How brains weigh reward against danger. The bitter-beats-sugar rule is a simple, fully mapped example of a decision every animal makes. Flies are widely used to study how brains work because so much of their biology is shared with ours: most genes linked to human disease have a counterpart in the fly (Reiter et al. 2001, Genome Research ). Insect feeding. Knowing which taste signals stop an insect from eating is the basis of feeding deterrents. Whether this fly's wiring carries over to pest species would need testing in those species. What it doesn't tell us. This is a model of one female fly's brain, with no body, no hunger or thirst state and no chemical messengers. It shows what the wiring can do, not everything a living fly does.

title: What we infer and why it matters (Neuron Silencing Screen)
text: id="infer">What we infer, and why it matters What these results tell us The feeding circuit has backups. Of 286 neurons switched off one at a time, only 8 lowered the tongue signal by more than 20%. For most neurons the signal simply finds another way to the tongue. That kind of redundancy is how a brain stays working when single cells fail. Drinking has more bottlenecks than eating. 7 of the 8 "needed" neurons matter for water, only 2 for sugar. In this brain, the sugar signal travels on many parallel roads; the water signal leans on a few key cells. A few cells are true chokepoints. Switching off "Roundup" #2 nearly silences drinking (98% drop) and "Clavicle" cuts it by 84%. In the map you can see the route collapse. Three new candidates. CB0192, CB0051 and CB0501 are predicted to be needed for drinking, and we found no living-fly test of them. These are new, testable predictions. How this can help in the real world Where to look first. Testing every neuron in a living fly takes years. A screen like this narrows 286 candidates down to 3 untested ones a lab could check next, saving time and animals. A method that scales. The same switch-off-and-watch approach works for any behaviour with a known motor neuron, and for any other brain once it has been mapped. Understanding thirst. Knowing which few cells carry the "drink" signal helps explain how brains control fluid intake, a basic survival system every animal shares in some form. What it doesn't tell us. These are predictions, not facts. When we checked this brain against known results it scored 10 of 15, and its misses were exactly this kind of single-neuron question. Each of the 8 is a strong lead that still needs a living-fly experiment.

title: The worm (C. elegans), second organism
text: The lab's second organism is the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, about 1 mm long, the first animal whose complete wiring diagram was mapped. Every adult hermaphrodite has the same 302 named neurons. The Worm page shows all 302 in 3D with every neuron-to-neuron connection: 2,973 chemical links and 849 pairs joined by electrical links (gap junctions). Neurons are sensory (blue), interneurons (amber), motor (pink) or role unknown. Click a neuron to see who it sends to and receives from. Famous circuits: gentle touch (Chalfie et al. 1985: front touch neurons ALM and AVM feed AVD and AVA, which drive backing up; back touch neurons PLM feed PVC and AVB, which drive forward movement) and the nerve ring hubs (AIB, AIY, AIZ, RIA, RIM, AVA, AVB). Data: neuron shapes from the Virtual Worm 3D model by Grove and Sternberg (WormBase, Caltech, public domain), converted to NeuroML by OpenWorm (c302, MIT licence); the shapes are a hand-built model matched to known anatomy, not traced from one scan. Wiring: Cook et al. 2019, Nature 571:63, as packaged by OpenWorm c302. Experiments on the worm are in progress; they need their own calibration test against real-worm results first.

title: Lab notebook DS1: Discovery Screen 1: which neurons does the fly need to eat and to drink?
text: Discovery screen Question: If one neuron is switched off, can the fly still eat (sugar) or drink (water)? Why: Most of these neurons have never been switched off in a living fly. The simulation can point a real lab to the few worth testing. Known from real flies: Method: The 200 most active neurons when sugar neurons fire at 100/s plus the 200 most active when water neurons fire at 200/s (from the round 1 records), leaving out the sugar and water sensors themselves and MN9: 286 neurons. Silence each candidate on its own (all its outgoing connections set to zero, as in the published code) and run sugar 100/s, then water 200/s. 10 repeats each for the screen. Every neuron scored 'needed' is then re-run with 30 repeats, and only the 30-repeat result is reported. Pass mark: A neuron is 'needed' for eating (or drinking) if silencing it lowers MN9's firing by more than 20% compared with the unsilenced run with the same repeats (the 2024 study's threshold). Each predicted neuron is marked 'tested in the 2024 study' if it appears in that study's named neuron lists, otherwise 'no living-fly test known to us'. We do not claim no one has ever tested it. written 2026-11-03 15:27 UTC Results: OK 286 neurons switched off one at a time; 8 predicted needed (confirmed with 30 repeats). | OK "Roundup" #1: eating 35% lower · Moderate lead | OK "Roundup" #2: eating 27% lower, drinking 98% lower · Strong lead | OK CB0192 #2: drinking 41% lower · Moderate lead | OK CB0051: drinking 55% lower · Strong lead | OK "Rattle": drinking 30% lower · Moderate lead | OK "Bract": drinking 34% lower · Moderate lead | OK CB0501: drinking 43% lower · Moderate lead | OK "Clavicle": drinking 84% lower · Strong lead Conclusion: 8 neurons predicted needed: 7 for drinking, 2 for eating (Roundup #2 for both). For most neurons the signal finds another route, so the feeding circuit has backups. How sure: On known single-neuron silencing results, the model matched 2 of 4 when whole cell types were silenced (round 1, E6) and 3 of 4 one cell at a time in this screen (G2N-1 only just). Even a strong lead is a hypothesis. Discovery: Potential discovery: 3 predictions (CB0192 #2, CB0051, CB0501) about neurons with no real-fly test known to us. They need a living-fly experiment to become a discovery.

title: Lab notebook PD1: Parkinson's mechanisms 1: what losing dopamine neurons does to the fly brain's wiring
text: Exploratory analysis (brain disease) Question: When dopamine neurons are lost, as in fruit-fly models of Parkinson's disease, which neurons and brain regions lose their dopamine input, how quickly, and where are the single points of failure? Why: In Parkinson's disease dopamine neurons die. Fly models of the disease lose them too. Mapping where their signal goes shows which parts of the brain depend on them and how well backed up they are. Known from real flies: Method: PPL1 first: the 16 PPL1 neurons lost one at a time (a cluster often reported vulnerable in fly Parkinson's models), then the rest at random. PAM only: PAM neurons lost at random, 0 to 100%. All dopamine neurons at random, 0 to 100% in 10% steps. Random orders use fixed seeds (10 orders); results report the average and range. For every neuron that receives dopamine-neuron connections: the share of its dopamine input synapses that remain. Grouped by FlyWire cell class and by brain region (neuropil). Neurons that lose half or more of their dopamine input, at each stage. Single points of failure: neurons whose dopamine input comes from 2 or fewer dopamine neurons. Fast-signal check with the published brain model (Shiu et al. 2024 settings): all 331 dopamine neurons removed, sugar 100/s and water 200/s, 30 repeats; change in MN9 firing. Pass mark: No pass mark: there is no real-fly measurement of this kind to check against. The analysis plan was written before it was run. written 2026-11-03 20:26 UTC Results: OK 331 dopamine neurons (PAM 307, PPL1 16, PPL2 8) send 61,099 synapses to 3,522 other neurons. | OK Single points of failure: 3,112 of 3,522 receiving neurons get dopamine from 2 or fewer dopamine neurons. | OK PPL1 first, then the rest, 166 dopamine neurons lost: 2,964 neurons lose half or more of their dopamine input (range over 10 orders 2,693-3,269); average input left 17%. | OK PPL1 first, then the rest, 331 dopamine neurons lost: 3,522 neurons lose half or more of their dopamine input (range over 10 orders 3,522-3,522); average input left 0%. | OK PAM only, 154 dopamine neurons lost: 215 neurons lose half or more of their dopamine input (range over 10 orders 151-290); average input left 93%. | OK PAM only, 307 dopamine neurons lost: 493 neurons lose half or more of their dopamine input (range over 10 orders 493-493); average input left 86%. | OK All at random, 166 dopamine neurons lost: 1,411 neurons lose half or more of their dopamine input (range over 10 orders 840-2,648); average input left 60%. | OK All at random, 331 dopamine neurons lost: 3,522 neurons lose half or more of their dopamine input (range over 10 orders 3,522-3,522); average input left 0%. | OK Fast-signal check: all dopamine neurons removed; MN9 to sugar 61.57 -> 61.57, to water 30.7 -> 30.7 per second. Dopamine neurons firing to taste in this model: 0. Conclusion: A few dopamine neurons reach very many targets (the 16 PPL1 neurons reach most of the receiving neurons), most targets have almost no backup, and most dopamine synapses land in the mushroom body, the learning centre. The fast taste reflex does not depend on dopamine neurons in this model. How sure: High for the wiring counts (read directly from the FlyWire data); exploratory for what they mean for the disease. Dopamine in real brains mostly changes how strongly other neurons are connected (for example, it drives learning in the mushroom body) and acts slowly; the simulation treats it as a fast signal. This analysis maps WHERE the dopamine signal would be lost and how robust each target is; it does not simulate the disease chemistry (such as alpha-synuclein), cell death itself, or behaviour. Exploratory: there is no real-fly measurement of this kind to check it against. Discovery: Exploratory mechanism map; no discovery claimed. It points to where dopamine loss would be felt first and where to look in future simulations that include dopamine's slow effects.

title: How sure are we about predictions (confidence levels)
text: Each Neuron Silencing Screen prediction was re-run 30 times with paired random inputs; the 95% range of the drop comes from resampling those runs. Clear in the simulation if the 95% range of the drop (from 30 paired runs) stays above the 20% "needed" line. Large effect if the drop is 50% or more; moderate if 20-50%. Levels: Strong lead: clear and large; Moderate lead: clear, moderate size; Weak lead: the 95% range dips below the 20% line. Track record: On known single-neuron silencing results, the model matched 2 of 4 when whole cell types were silenced (round 1, E6) and 3 of 4 one cell at a time in this screen (G2N-1 only just). Even a strong lead is a hypothesis. Rule written 2026-11-03, after the screen; it labels results and changes none of them.

text: The What's next page lists: predictions waiting for a real-fly test (the 8 Neuron Silencing Screen predictions with confidence levels; 3 new discovery candidates CB0051, CB0192, CB0501 with no real-fly test known to us), how a fly lab could test one (switch the neuron off genetically, offer water or sugar, count proboscis extensions, compare with controls), work in progress (experiments on Maxime and Hagrid; worm calibration test), planned fly experiments (more behaviours such as grooming, escape, walking and courtship song; switching single neurons on; adding chemical messengers to the model) and candidate organisms (fruit fly larva, Winding et al. 2023 Science; mouse visual cortex, MICrONS 2025 Nature; human cortex fragment, Shapson-Coe et al. 2024 Science).

title: Parkinson's mechanisms (dopamine neuron loss)
text: The Parkinson's page maps, in the FlyWire brain's wiring, where the dopamine signal goes and what is cut off as dopamine neurons die, as in fly Parkinson's models (Feany and Bender 2000; Whitworth et al. 2005, PPL1 loss; Riemensperger et al. 2013, PAM loss). 331 dopamine neurons (FlyWire class DAN: PAM 307, PPL1 16, PPL2 8) send 61099 synapses to 3522 neurons; about 69% land in the mushroom body (learning centre). The 16 PPL1 neurons reach 2519 neurons; 3112 of 3522 receiving neurons get dopamine from 2 or fewer dopamine neurons (little backup). Removing all dopamine neurons did not change the taste reflex in the simulation (no dopamine neurons fire to taste in the model). Exploratory: it maps wiring, not disease chemistry; dopamine's slow effects are not yet simulated. PPM and PAL dopamine clusters are not included (not labelled DAN in FlyWire).
